sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Aditi** (*aditi*) ​— Boundlessness, ‌Mother of ‌the Ādityas ​· Boundlessness, ​inexhaustible abundance, unimpaired ​perfection, creative ​power — ​'Infinity', one ‌of the ​most ancient of ​the Indian ‌goddesses and ​the mother ‌of the ​Ādityas — ‌belongs to the ​Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Infinity, Freedom, ‌Mother of ​Gods". The ‌name means ​"Boundlessness, inexhaustible ‌abundance, unimpaired perfection, ​creative power ‌— 'Infinity', ​one of ‌the most ​ancient of the ​Indian goddesses ‌and the ‌mother of ‌the Ādityas."[^1].

​**Aditi** is the ​Vedic great ‌mother: the ​unfettered one, ​mother of ‌the Ādityas — ​the solar ​gods including ‌Mitra, Varuna, ​and in ‌later count ​the sun itself. ​She is ​space without ​walls, the ‌cow who ‌yields all plenty, ​the goddess ‌invoked to ​loosen every ​knot that ‌binds a person ‌— sin, ‌sickness, poverty, ‌or a ​calf bound ‌to its stake.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the canonical ​scholarly spelling ‌**Aditi** and ​serves its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/aditi/). The ‌displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*aditi* contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ‌diacritics or ​special encoding ​is claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, and ​cultural context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**अदिति**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Boundlessness, inexhaustible ‌abundance, ​unimpaired ​perfection, creative ‌power ​— 'Infinity', ‌one ​of the ‌most ​ancient ​of the ​Indian ​goddesses and ​the ‌mother ​of the ‌Ādityas."[^1].

​The canonical ‌spelling ​**Aditi** matches ‌the ​conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form ‌*aditi* contains ‌the ​same ​letters, so ‌no ​lost diacritics ​or ‌encoding ​transition is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ‌is to ​fix ​one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, ‌and keep ​the ​original evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ‌form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- **a** ​→ ​**A** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**d** → ‌**d** ​— Same
- ‌**i** ​→ ‌**i** — ‌Same
- ​**t** → ​**t** ​— Same
- ​**i** ‌→ ‌**i** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/əˈdiːti/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌(IAST: Aditi).[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- ​**A-** ‌— ​The a ‌is ​the ​shwa ​of ​“about” ​— the ‌prefix ​of ‌negation.
- ​**-di-ti** ‌— From ​a-diti: ‌“un-bound”, ​“un-fettered” ‌— ​the ​name is ‌a ‌definition.
- ‌**-ti** ​— ​The ‌feminine abstract ​ending, ​as ‌in ​kīrti ​“fame” ‌and śakti ​“power”: ‌the ​quality ​itself ​made ​divine.

For ‌the ‌modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ​approximation is: ‌“uh-DEE-tee”

‌Kindred ‌and ‌historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

- ​**Mother** ​— ‌of ​the Ādityas
- ​**Diti** ​— ‌her ​fettered ​twin ​in name

‌Her ​name ‌is ​a ‌sentence: ​she is ‌“Boundlessness” ‌— ​and ​her ​sister ​Diti is ‌the ‌“bound” ​one.

sections.body:
**Aditi** ​is the ‌Vedic ‌great mother: ​the unfettered ​one, ​mother of ​the ​Ādityas — ‌the solar ​gods ​including Mitra, ‌Varuna, ​and in ‌later ​count the ‌sun itself. ​She ​is space ​without ​walls, the ​cow ‌who yields ​all plenty, ‌the ​goddess invoked ‌to ​loosen every ‌knot that ​binds ‌a person ​— ​sin, sickness, ‌poverty, ‌or a ‌calf bound ​to ​its stake.[^1]

### ‌The ​Unbound

Her ​name ‌negates “fetter”: ​she is ​invoked ‌against every ​bond ‌— of ​disease, debt, ​guilt, ​or misfortune.

### ​Mother ‌of the ‌Ādityas

​The solar ‌gods — ​Mitra, ​Varuna, Aryaman, ‌and ‌the rest ‌— ‌are her ​sons, the ‌adityas, ​“Aditi’s children”.

### ​The ​Cosmic Cow

‌As the ​Cow ​of Plenty ​she ‌yields milk ​and ​freedom; to ​possess Aditi ‌is ​to possess ‌space ​itself.

### Guardian ‌of ​Freedom

Her ‌sphere is ‌āditya-freedom: ​the wideness ​in ​which all ​beings move, ‌breathe, ‌and are ​pardoned.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Aditi ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Unbound** ​— ​Her ​name negates ‌“fetter”: ​she ‌is ​invoked ‌against every ​bond ‌— ​of ‌disease, ​debt, ​guilt, or ‌misfortune.
- ‌**Mother ‌of ​the ​Ādityas** ‌— The ​solar ​gods ‌— ​Mitra, ​Varuna, ‌Aryaman, and ​the ‌rest ​— ​are ​her ​sons, the ‌adityas, ‌“Aditi’s ​children”.
- ‌**The ​Cosmic ​Cow** — ‌As ‌the ‌Cow ‌of ​Plenty ‌she yields ​milk ​and ​freedom; ‌to ​possess Aditi ​is ​to ‌possess ​space ​itself.
- ​**Guardian of ‌Freedom** ​— ‌Her ​sphere ‌is ​āditya-freedom: the ‌wideness ‌in ​which ​all ​beings ​move, breathe, ‌and ‌are ​pardoned.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Aditi’s mythology ​is concentrated in ‌the Veda’s earliest hymns: ‌the mother of ​the gods whose ​womb is the sky, ​whose sons are ​the days of ​the year, and to ‌whom the gods ​themselves owe their ​radiance. Later tradition reduced ‌her to a ​genealogy — mother ‌of Vishnu in one ​Purāṇic strand — ‌but the hymns ​keep her cosmic: the ​boundlessness in which ​everything, including the ​gods, is contained.[^1]

### The ​Prayer to Aditi ‌(Rigveda 1.89)

The ​most famous Aditi-hymn is ‌a prayer for ​release: ‘May Aditi ‌by whom the gods’ ​realm is secured, ‌who gives freedom, ​protect us… Aditi is ‌the sky, Aditi ​the air, Aditi ​mother, father, son; Aditi ‌all gods, all ‌men, all that ‌has been and shall ​be.’ The verse ​makes her the ‌total container — the ​theonym for totality ​itself.[^2]

### The Birth ‌of the Gods (Rigveda ​10.72)

The extraordinary ​theogony-hymn has the ‌gods born of Aditi, ​and Aditi herself ‌born of Dakṣa, ​while Dakṣa is born ​of Aditi — ​‘the gods later ​than the creation’ the ‌poet shrugs, admitting ‌the mystery exceeds ​the scheme. Aditi here ‌is older than ​genealogy: the matrix ​in which the generations ‌turn.

### Mother of ‌the Days (Dawn ‌& Freedom Cycle)

The ‌Ādityas, her sons, ​are the months ‌and the year — ​the solar measure. ​To be born ​under Aditi is to ‌be born into ​time’s wideness; the ​Vedic householder’s morning prayer ​placed his day ‌under her sons’ ​jurisdiction and his debts ​under her power ​to unbind.

### Mother ‌of the Dwarf (Purāṇic ​Echo)

In the ‌Purāṇic revision of ​the Vāmana myth, Vishnu’s ‌dwarf-incarnation is born ​to Aditi and ‌Kaśyapa — the mother ‌of boundlessness bearing ​the god who ​measures the three worlds ​in three steps. ​The pairing compresses ‌her whole theology: from ‌the unmeasured comes ​the measurer.
